title: Isogeny theorem and root-exponent criteria for split reductive groups
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure], of characteristic exponent $p$ ($p=1$ in characteristic zero). Let $(G_1,S_1),(G_0,S_0)$ be split reductive $F$-group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] with split maximal tori and reduced root data $(M_i,R_i,M_i^\vee,R_i^\vee)$ as in [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure], where $M_i=X^*(S_i)$ and $M_i^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbf Z}(M_i,\mathbf Z)$. Suppose $u:M_0\to M_1$ is injective with finite cokernel, and there are a bijection $b:R_1\to R_0$ and numbers $q_\alpha\in\{p^e:e\geq0\}$ such that $u(b(\alpha))=q_\alpha\alpha$ and $u^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=q_\alpha b(\alpha)^\vee$ for every $\alpha\in R_1$, where $u^\vee$ is restriction of integer-valued functionals. Then there exists a surjective homomorphism $g:G_1\to G_0$ with finite scheme-theoretic kernel, with $g(S_1)=S_0$ and $(g|_{S_1})^*=u$. For every such isogeny inducing $u$, the kernel is central if and only if every $q_\alpha=1$, and $g$ is an isomorphism if and only if every $q_\alpha=1$ and $u$ is an isomorphism of abelian groups. Finite means finite-dimensional coordinate algebra; central means commuting with every group element after every commutative $F$-algebra extension. No reducedness of the kernel or prime-to-characteristic condition on the cokernel is assumed.

source.place: Definitions 23.1--23.2, printed pp.483--484; Proposition 23.5, printed pp.485--486; Theorem 23.9, printed p.487; full isogeny theorem 23.25, printed pp.492--493.

proof.text: The character antiduality [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] gives the unique torus homomorphism $h:S_1\to S_0$ with $h^*=u$. In the group-algebra descriptions, $h^*$ sends $e_m$ to $e_{u(m)}$. Coset representatives for $M_1/u(M_0)$ give a finite free basis of $F[M_1]$ over $F[M_0]$, of positive rank. Thus this map is faithfully flat, and [lem-weil-pbc-faithfully-flat-surjective-spectrum] makes the associated map of spectra surjective. Its identity fibre has algebra $F[M_1]/(e_{u(m)}-1)_m=F[M_1/u(M_0)]$, which is finite-dimensional. In particular $h$ has finite kernel and image $S_0$. The given dual relation says precisely $h\circ\alpha^\vee=b(\alpha)^\vee\circ(t\mapsto t^{q_\alpha})$, since the perfect character pairing separates cocharacters.

source.place: Theorem 12.9, pp.233--234; Definitions 23.1--23.2, pp.483--484: passage between torus and lattice maps.

proof.text: Choose a Borel containing $S_1$ and its positive roots and simple base $\Phi_1^+,\Delta_1$ [lem-sfb-reductive-borel-pair-structure]. Choose a regular cocharacter $\lambda_1$ defining this Borel by [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description], and put $\lambda_0=h\lambda_1$. Then $\langle b(\alpha),\lambda_0\rangle=q_\alpha\langle\alpha,\lambda_1\rangle$, so $\lambda_0$ is regular and defines a Borel of $G_0$ whose positive roots are $b(\Phi_1^+)$. The bases correspond: under $u_{\mathbf Q}$ their positive cones coincide, since every root is carried to a positive multiple of its corresponding root. In a cone freely spanned by a simple-root base, the extremal rays are exactly the simple-root rays (uniqueness of coefficients). Thus the two simple bases have corresponding rays; reducedness permits only one positive root on each ray, so $\Delta_0=b(\Delta_1)$. Similarly $b(-\alpha)=-b(\alpha)$ and $q_{-\alpha}=q_\alpha$ follow by applying $u_{\mathbf Q}^{-1}$ and reducedness. If the roots are empty, both groups are their maximal tori by the empty-root clause of [lem-sfb-regular-cocharacter-borel-description], so $h$ already supplies the desired map.

source.place: Proposition 23.4, p.484, with its positive-cone argument made explicit; rank-zero paragraph before Proposition 23.14, p.489.

proof.text: For $\alpha\in\Delta_1$ form $G_{1,\alpha}$ and $G_{0,b(\alpha)}$ using [lem-sfb-reductive-rank-one-reflections]. To see their roots, a character is trivial on the largest subtorus of $\ker\alpha$ exactly when it is a rational multiple of $\alpha$ (character antiduality [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality]). Differentiating the defining centralizer equations selects precisely those weight spaces. Ambient reducedness then leaves exactly $\pm\alpha$ and $\pm b(\alpha)$, with the same ambient tori; the coroots agree by the reflection-identity uniqueness in the rank-one-reflections node. The equations $u(b(\alpha))=q_\alpha\alpha$ and $u^\vee(\alpha^\vee)=q_\alpha b(\alpha)^\vee$, together with step 2 for negative roots, verify the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-rank-one-frobenius-extension]. It yields $f_\alpha:G_{1,\alpha}\to G_{0,b(\alpha)}$ restricting to the SAME $h$, mapping both opposite root subgroups onto their counterparts, with exponent $q_\alpha$.

source.place: 23.16, p.490, applying Proposition 23.14 to the rank-one subgroups of Theorem 21.11.

proof.text: Take the reduced closed subgroup $L\subseteq G_1\times_FG_0$ generated by the torus graph and the graphs of the $f_\alpha$. All the hypotheses of [lem-sfb-compatible-rank-one-graph-geometry] hold: step 2 gives the bijection of simple bases; step 1 gives the torus character condition; step 3 gives the two root images and the common torus restriction. Therefore $L$ is reductive, $T_L=\Gamma_h$ is maximal, and the first torus projection $a:T_L\xrightarrow{\sim}S_1$ identifies their FULL root data, not just the tangent characters. Write $p_1:L\to G_1$ and $p_0:L\to G_0$ for the projections. Apply [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] to $p_1$: its root exponents are all one, its torus restriction is $a$, and its kernel coordinates are all trivial. Thus $p_1$ is faithfully flat with trivial scheme-theoretic kernel.

source.place: 23.17--23.24 and the final paragraph of 23.18, pp.490--492; the big-cell trivial-kernel calculation of Proposition 23.5.

proof.text: A faithfully flat affine group homomorphism with trivial kernel is invertible here directly by [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal]: the identity of $L$ kills $\ker p_1$, so it factors as $j p_1=\mathrm{id}_L$; uniqueness applied to $p_1:L\to G_1$ then gives $p_1j=\mathrm{id}_{G_1}$. Define $g=p_0j$. On tori $j$ is $a^{-1}$, so $g|_{S_1}=h$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] to this already constructed homomorphism: its character map is $u$, and the root and coroot equations are the given hypotheses. It follows that $g$ is faithfully flat, hence surjective, with finite scheme-theoretic kernel.

source.place: Completion of 23.18, p.492, and Lemma 23.10, p.487; Theorem 5.13 and Proposition 5.43 (affine quotient universal property).

proof.text: Now let $g$ be ANY isogeny in the statement with torus character map $u$. Apply [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] again, using the prescribed $b,q_\alpha$; reducedness makes this correspondence and these exponents unique, since two positive multiples of roots on the same ray must involve the same root. Suppose its kernel $K$ is central. By the scheme-theoretic equality $C_{G_1}(S_1)=S_1$ of [lem-sfb-reductive-torus-self-centralizer], $K\subseteq S_1$. Hence $K\cap U_{1,\alpha}$ is trivial. But the root formula identifies this intersection with $\operatorname{Spec}F[z]/(z^{q_\alpha})$. Its coordinate algebra has basis $1,z,\ldots,z^{q_\alpha-1}$; it is the trivial group scheme only if $q_\alpha=1$. This detects nonreduced root kernels as well as reduced ones.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, final two paragraphs, p.486, using Theorem 21.84 scheme-theoretically.

proof.text: Conversely, suppose all $q_\alpha=1$. The kernel-coordinate isomorphism [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] now identifies $K$ with $\ker h\subseteq S_1$. For every $F$-algebra $A$ and $k\in K(A)$, the equation $u(b(\alpha))=\alpha$ gives $\alpha(k)=b(\alpha)(h(k))=1$. The conjugation formula of [lem-sfb-reductive-root-subgroup-parametrizations] says that $k$ commutes with every root subgroup, and it commutes with the torus. Thus the two morphisms $K\times G_1\to G_1$, $(k,x)\mapsto kxk^{-1}$ and $(k,x)\mapsto x$, agree on $K\times C_1$, where $C_1$ is the dense big cell in the kernel-coordinate node. This equality extends to $K\times G_1$: $G_1$ is integral by [lem-sfb-bruhat-longest-cell-charts], so restriction from its coordinate ring to the dense open $C_1$ is injective; tensoring this injection with the $F$-vector space $F[K]$ remains injective. Comparing the pullbacks of each function of the affine target proves equality on all $K\times G_1$. This is centrality over every algebra, even when $K$ is nonreduced.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, p.486: centrality when all root maps are isomorphisms; scheme-theoretic density elaboration using Theorem 21.84 and formula (144).

proof.text: If $g$ is an isomorphism, its kernel is trivial, hence central, so step 6 gives $q_\alpha=1$. Its restriction $h:S_1\to S_0$ has trivial kernel; the group-algebra computation in step 1 then gives $F[M_1/u(M_0)]=F$, so the coset basis forces $M_1/u(M_0)=0$. Thus $u$ is an isomorphism. Conversely, if all $q_\alpha=1$ and $u$ is an isomorphism, character antiduality [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality] makes $h$ an isomorphism. The kernel coordinates [lem-sfb-root-monomial-kernel-coordinates] give $K=1$. The same quotient-universal-property argument as in step 5, now using [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal] for $g$, constructs its two-sided inverse. The empty-root case has the same conclusion; every torus kernel is central because a torus is commutative.

source.place: Proposition 23.5, last paragraph, p.486; Definitions 23.1--23.2 and Theorem 12.9.
